title: Going years without the tuba and loving the bass and tuba equally
summary: He says time away from an instrument does not matter after early practice, and he loves bass, tuba and writing equally.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So you went several years without playing a tuba?

Oh yeah. Several times I've been several years without touching the horn. But it hasn't seemed to matter. I can put the horn down for a month, and pick it up, and you wouldn't know the difference. I would know. But I have an affinity for the horn and the bass. Like, right now I'm going through... Well, I spent a month in Europe, and I didn't touch my bass. I just played the horn.
So I came back, and my first recording was on bass. Nobody knew I hadn't played it for a month except me.

But I find when you spend the earlier years of your life like I did... I would get up before daylight every day, and practice for hours. So I think when you spend enough time at anything, it never leaves you. You just have to take a little refresher.
Would you say that you have equal love for the two instruments?
That's the way I feel from listening to you. Listening to you play; I don't mean just listening to you talk. And I wondered if that...

It's true. It's true. I love both equally, and I try to spend as much time on one as I do the other. And also my writing... That's sort of a triumvirate of love there. I love to write, too. So I have to try to divide my time where I can keep up on all these things, and still manage to have a little fun on the side. But in reality, it's all fun. I consider, never having really worked in my life, I've made a fairly decent living -- but it's never been work, because I enjoy every moment of all of it. And there has been times...
